summary: Lists requirements for a Web Distributed Authoring and Versioning protocol, including remote editing, locking to avoid overwrites, link management, simple metadata, container data types and versioning. It is informational and is a wish list, not a protocol.

eli5.summary: It is a list of things people wanted web pages to do, like letting several people edit files without erasing each other's work.

questions: what is the lost update problem
subtitle: The wish list that shaped WebDAV: remote editing on the Web without overwriting each other's work.

tldr.problem: Web standards of the time could save a file to a server, but could not stop two authors overwriting each other, move changes efficiently, manage links between non-HTML files, or track versions.
tldr.mechanism: The WebDAV working group lists requirements for extensions to HTTP: properties, links, locking, reservations, source retrieval, partial write, copy and move, collections, versioning, variants, security and internationalization.
tldr.outcome: It is a list of requirements, not a protocol, and it deliberately avoids proposing an implementation.

today: RFC 2291 is Informational and has not been obsoleted or updated. It records the requirements the WebDAV working group aimed to satisfy, not a protocol itself.

sections.title: Why Authoring Needs More Than HTTP
sections.content:
Existing Web standards let tools load, edit and save (publish) content on a remote server, and authoring tools and word processors already do this. But the memo says experience shows these tools cannot meet users' needs with the facilities of Web standards. The result is either delayed authoring features or nonstandard HTTP extensions that are not interoperable, with each vendor's service needing a different interface.

The WebDAV working group (Distributed Authoring and Versioning) therefore lists functionality that should be standardized as extensions to HTTP, described as far as possible without prescribing an implementation. The consensus covers properties, links, locking, reservations, retrieval of unprocessed source, partial write, name space manipulation, collections, versioning, variants, security and internationalization.

Several principles cut across all the features. Any WebDAV client should work with any WebDAV-compliant server, and clients should be simple to build. A compliant server should be able to serve ordinary non-WebDAV clients with valid HTTP 1.1 responses, and should work with existing resources and URIs without mandatory extra information in document formats.

The extensions must work in a distributed, replicated environment: version trees may be split across servers and collections may have members on different servers. They should keep client-server interactions to a minimum, must define how existing methods such as PUT and DELETE behave with the new kinds of objects, and should not preclude carrying the protocol by other means, particularly email.
sections.eli5: Everyone invented their own way to share edited files, and none of the ways worked together. This list asks for one shared way.

sections.title: Properties and Links
sections.content:
The first requirement is that it must be possible to create, modify, read and delete arbitrary properties (named descriptive information) on resources of any media type. Examples include author, title, publisher, subject, usage constraints and PICS ratings. They support searching, enforcing copyrights and catalog entries for objects not yet available electronically.

The second is typed links between resources of any media type, with the same create, modify, read and delete operations. HTML already has the LINK element, but it only works for HTML, while similar support is needed for bitmap images and other types. Links could support printing a multi-resource document in order or jumping to a resource's access control page.
sections.eli5: Properties are sticky notes on a file saying who made it and what it is. Links are strings connecting related files, even pictures.

sections.title: Locking and Reservations
sections.content:
Without protection, two people saving to one URI can silently overwrite each other, the lost update problem. The memo requires write locks that restrict modification to a specific person, a way to query who holds locks, and a way to remove a lock. A lock must be possible without retrieving the resource, and locking several resources on one server must be atomic, so that two people competing for the same set do not end up with the locks split between them.

Reservations are separate. A reservation registers an intent to edit, so others can see who is about to edit and coordinate out-of-band. It carries no access restrictions, and a write lock does not imply editing. Reservations can be queried and released.
sections.eli5: A lock is a 'do not touch' sign on a file. A reservation is a note saying 'I plan to edit this later', which warns people without stopping them.

sections.title: Source, Partial Writes, Name Space Operations and Collections
sections.content:
Anyone authorized to edit must be able to retrieve a resource's unprocessed source, since what a server stores can differ from what GET returns. Examples are server side include directives, SGML converted to HTML on the fly, or a word processor's native format converted to HTML.

After editing, a client must be able to write only the changes instead of the whole resource, which matters over slow or distant links. The memo mentions insert and delete style updates.

Copy and move or rename must be done by the server without the client loading and resaving. After a copy, changing one resource must not change the other, and after a move the old location must no longer work.

A collection is a resource that contains other resources, including other collections, directly or by reference. If a resource is a direct member, name space operations such as copy, move and delete on the collection also apply to it. For a member by reference, they affect only the reference.

Required operations are listing a collection, making a collection, adding a resource directly or by reference, and removing a resource. These support "Save As..." dialog boxes, tree visualizations and document management systems exposed on the Web. Where listing makes no sense for a URL, a server could answer with 405 Method Not Allowed.
sections.eli5:
If you fix one typo, you should send just the fix, not the whole book. Copying or renaming a file should happen on the server, not by downloading it and uploading it again.

A collection is a folder. You can list what is in it, make new ones, and put things in or take them out.

sections.title: Versioning
sections.content:
Versions eventually become frozen and immutable, so retrieving a frozen version always returns the same content or an error. Versions form a version graph, a directed acyclic graph where each version is derived from its predecessors, allowing branching and merging. Typically a checkout combines reservation, locking and retrieval, and a checkin combines writing and releasing the lock and reservation.

Requirements include referring to a whole graph and to each member, telling whether a resource is a graph or member, a server-defined default member, finding a member's graphs, navigating to root, predecessors, successors and default, retrieving the full version topology in a standard format, and unique version identifiers across a graph. A client may propose an identifier, which the server may refuse, and can attach version-specific properties such as comments.
sections.eli5: Versioning is like saving every draft of an essay. Old drafts never change, and you can see which draft came from which.

sections.title: Variants, Security and Internationalization
sections.content:
Authors must be able to send variants to the server, such as different formats, languages or output devices, and to describe how they relate to the parent resource. Detailed requirements for variants were to be developed in a separate document.

For security, the specification should say how WebDAV works with existing authentication schemes, refer to a separate access control work in progress, and list a minimal set of security protocols that all compliant clients and servers must support to ensure authenticity, privacy and integrity of messages. For internationalization, information for users must follow the IETF Character Set Policy (RFC 2277), covering character sets and language tagging.
sections.eli5: People need to send different versions of a page, for different languages and screens. Everything must be safe to send and work with any alphabet.
